words.exampleSentence: The platform team added ResourceQuotas to every team namespace after one team's memory-leaking microservice consumed all available memory across the shared cluster, causing OOM evictions for other teams.

codeExample.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-alpha-quota
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 40Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    pods: "50"
    count/deployments.apps: "20"
    count/services: "20"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"

words.etymology: Resource from Latin resourcere ('to spring back'); quota from Medieval Latin quota ('how large a share') — a declared proportional allocation of cluster capacity to a namespace.

words.shortDefinition: Namespace policy that sets default and maximum resource requests/limits for containers that don't specify their own.
words.simpleDefinition: A LimitRange sets per-container guardrails within a namespace: default resource requests and limits (injected into containers that specify none), minimum bounds (no container may request less than this), and maximum bounds (no container may request more than this). It prevents both the zero-resource pod that starves the scheduler and the runaway pod that claims an entire node.
words.longDefinition: LimitRange is enforced by the LimitRanger admission controller. It operates at the individual container level (and optionally at the pod and PersistentVolumeClaim level), not the namespace aggregate level — that is ResourceQuota's domain. The four fields per type are: default (the limit injected when none is specified), defaultRequest (the request injected when none is specified), max (the upper bound — a container requesting or declaring a limit above this is rejected), and min (the lower bound — a container requesting below this is rejected). The interaction with ResourceQuota is important: when a ResourceQuota is active in a namespace, every pod must have resource requests and limits set; if an application team submits a pod with no resources specified and a LimitRange with defaultRequest and default exists, the LimitRanger injects the defaults before the Quota admission controller validates the namespace totals. This pairing — LimitRange for per-container defaults, ResourceQuota for namespace totals — is the standard multi-tenant Kubernetes resource management pattern. LimitRange also applies to persistent storage: a PVC min/max spec prevents teams from requesting 0Gi or 10Ti volumes.
words.connector: Think of LimitRange like a hotel's room policy — there is a minimum stay (min request), a maximum stay (max request), and if you do not specify how long you are staying, you are automatically booked for the standard duration (default).
words.techContext: Without a LimitRange, a pod with no resource requests defined is a BestEffort QoS pod that the kernel will OOM-kill first under memory pressure. A LimitRange with a defaultRequest ensures every pod gets at least Burstable QoS, improving operational predictability.
words.exampleSentence: After deploying a LimitRange with a max memory of 4Gi, the intern's misconfigured pod that attempted to request 512Gi memory was rejected at admission time with a clear error message rather than scheduling and consuming the whole node.

codeExample.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: team-alpha
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: "500m"
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 8Gi
      min:
        cpu: "10m"
        memory: 32Mi

words.etymology: Limit from Latin limes ('boundary'); range from Old French renge ('row, line') — a declared spectrum of permissible resource values for containers in a namespace.

words.shortDefinition: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, then SIGKILL; preStop hook runs before SIGTERM.
words.simpleDefinition: When Kubernetes decides to terminate a pod — during a rolling update, node drain, or manual delete — it follows a defined sequence to give the application a chance to shut down cleanly: it removes the pod from Service endpoints, runs the preStop hook if configured, sends SIGTERM to containers, waits up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds, then sends SIGKILL to any survivors. Without proper graceful shutdown handling, in-flight requests are dropped.
words.longDefinition: The Kubernetes pod termination sequence is: (1) Pod is marked Terminating and removed from Endpoints/EndpointSlices of all Services — new traffic stops routing to it; (2) The preStop lifecycle hook executes if defined (exec command or HTTP GET); (3) SIGTERM is delivered to PID 1 of each container; (4) Kubernetes waits up to spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s) for containers to exit; (5) SIGKILL is sent to any containers still running, causing immediate termination. There is a critical race condition: there is propagation lag between the pod being removed from Endpoints and load-balancer rules converging. A preStop sleep of 5-15 seconds absorbs this lag so that SIGTERM is not delivered until the load balancer has stopped routing new connections. Application best practices: handle SIGTERM explicitly (stop accepting new connections, drain the request queue, flush buffers, exit cleanly with code 0); set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to comfortably exceed the preStop duration plus the slowest possible in-flight request; use exec-form ENTRYPOINT so the app receives SIGTERM directly rather than through a shell wrapper that may absorb the signal.
words.connector: Think of graceful shutdown like a restaurant calling 'last orders' — customers are notified the kitchen is closing (SIGTERM), have a defined window to finish their meals (grace period), and if anyone is still at the table after closing time, the lights are turned off regardless (SIGKILL).
words.techContext: The standard production preStop hook is a sleep 5 command to absorb endpoint propagation lag. terminationGracePeriodSeconds should be set to preStop duration + longest expected request duration + 10s buffer — commonly 60-120 seconds for databases.
words.exampleSentence: Before we added the preStop sleep hook, users experienced random 502 errors during rolling deployments as requests hit pods that had already received SIGTERM but were still listed as ready endpoints by the load balancer.

codeExample.code:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: my-registry/api:v2.0.0
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            # Allow load balancer to drain before SIGTERM
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
      # Application must handle SIGTERM:
      # - Stop accepting new connections
      # - Wait for in-flight requests to complete
      # - Exit 0

words.etymology: Graceful from Latin gratia ('favour, elegance') — implying a clean, ordered process; shutdown from 'shut' (Old English scyttan) + 'down' — the controlled cessation of a process.

words.shortDefinition: Automatic PV and backing disk creation when a PVC references a StorageClass, eliminating manual admin pre-provisioning.
words.simpleDefinition: Dynamic provisioning means you submit a PVC referencing a StorageClass, and Kubernetes automatically creates the backing cloud disk, the PersistentVolume object, and the PVC binding — no administrator involvement required. Before dynamic provisioning, admins had to manually pre-create every disk and PV before a workload could claim storage.
words.longDefinition: The dynamic provisioning flow: (1) Developer creates a PVC specifying storageClassName: fast-ssd; (2) The kube-controller-manager identifies the unbound PVC and its StorageClass; (3) The external-provisioner CSI sidecar issues a CreateVolume RPC to the CSI driver controller pod; (4) The CSI driver calls the cloud API to create the backing resource (e.g., AWS EBS CreateVolume, GCP CreateDisk); (5) The driver creates a PersistentVolume object with the volume handle and binding information; (6) The control plane binds the PV to the PVC; (7) The PVC transitions from Pending to Bound; (8) The pod can now be scheduled; the kubelet calls NodeStageVolume and NodePublishVolume to attach and mount the disk. When the PVC is deleted with reclaimPolicy: Delete, the external-provisioner issues a DeleteVolume RPC that deletes the backing disk. WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode defers step 3-6 until a pod using the PVC is actually scheduled, ensuring the disk is created in the same availability zone as the target node. Dynamic provisioning is the default in managed Kubernetes offerings (EKS, GKE, AKS) — cluster operators configure StorageClasses; application teams provision storage self-service without waiting for the operations team.
words.connector: Think of dynamic provisioning like a self-service office supply cabinet — you scan a barcode for what you need, the cabinet automatically orders a replacement and logs the consumption, rather than submitting a purchase request that takes days to fulfil.
words.techContext: A PVC stuck in Pending with the event 'waiting for a volume to be created, either by external provisioner or manually' means the CSI driver controller pod is unavailable or the cloud credentials are invalid — check the external-provisioner sidecar logs in the CSI controller pod.
words.exampleSentence: With dynamic provisioning and WaitForFirstConsumer, our StatefulSet could scale from 3 to 10 replicas in under 3 minutes — each new pod triggered automatic disk creation in the correct AZ without any platform team ticket.

codeExample.code:
# PVC triggers dynamic provisioning
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: redis-data-0
  namespace: caching
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-ssd   # references the StorageClass
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
# Result: CSI driver creates a 10Gi gp3 EBS volume
# and a PV automatically — no admin action needed

words.etymology: Dynamic from Greek dynamis ('power, force') — contrasted with static; provisioning from Latin provisio ('foresight, preparation') — automatic preparation of resources in response to demand.
